title: Triangles & the Pythagorean Theorem
sub: 180° in every triangle, and a² + b² = c²

steps.html:
Triangles

a + b + c = 180°
say: Today: triangles. First, the most important triangle fact of all.
Take any triangle and tear off its three corners. Put them side by side, and they always make a perfectly straight line.
A straight line is one hundred eighty degrees. So the three angles of every triangle add up to one hundred eighty degrees. Always.

steps.html: Two angles of a triangle are 72° and 38°. What is the third angle?
say: Two angles of a triangle are seventy-two and thirty-eight degrees. What is the third angle?
steps.okSay: Yes! One eighty minus seventy-two minus thirty-eight is seventy.
steps.no: 72 + 38 = 110 is just the two angles you were given. The third is 180 − 110 = 70°. Always finish by subtracting from 180.
steps.noSay: Not quite. Seventy-two plus thirty-eight is one-ten, but that's only two of the angles. The third angle is one eighty minus one-ten, which is seventy.

steps.html:
Triangle types

Rightone 90° angle (the little square)
Isosceles2 equal sides → the 2 angles at their base are equal too
Equilateral3 equal sides → every angle is 60°
say: Triangles come in a few types you should know by name.
A right triangle has one ninety degree angle, marked with a little square.
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and the two angles at the base of those sides are equal too.
An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so all three angles are sixty degrees. Sixty times three is one eighty.

steps.html: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 40°. What is each of the two equal base angles?
say: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of forty degrees. What is each of the two equal base angles?
steps.ok: Yes! 180 − 40 = 140 for both base angles together, and 140 ÷ 2 = 70°.
steps.okSay: Yes! One eighty minus forty is one forty. Split it into two equal angles: seventy each.
steps.no: 180 − 40 = 140 is shared by the two equal angles, so each is 140 ÷ 2 = 70°.
steps.noSay: Not quite. One eighty minus forty leaves one forty for the two base angles together. Split it in half: seventy degrees each.

steps.html:
The Pythagorean theorem (right triangles only)

legs a, bthe two sides that make the right angle
hypotenuse cacross from the right angle, always the longest
a2 + b2 = c29 + 16 = 25
say: Now the famous one: the Pythagorean theorem. It only works for right triangles.
The two sides that make the right angle are called legs. We'll call them a and b.
The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse, c. It's always the longest side.

Here's the magic. Build a square on each side. For a three, four, five triangle, the squares are nine, sixteen, and twenty-five. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five! So a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
Let's find a missing hypotenuse together. The legs are six and eight.

steps.say: Last step: take the square root.

steps.html:
Missing a leg? Subtract.

Missing the hypotenuse → ADD the squares.
Missing a leg → SUBTRACT: big square − small square.
hypotenuse 17, leg 15
172 − 152 = 289 − 225 = 64
√64 = 8
say: What if the hypotenuse is given and a leg is missing?
Here's the rule. Missing the hypotenuse? Add the squares. Missing a leg? Subtract: the big square minus the small square.
For example, hypotenuse seventeen and leg fifteen. Seventeen squared is two eighty-nine. Fifteen squared is two twenty-five. Subtract to get sixty-four. The square root is eight.

steps.html: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Find the other leg.
say: A right triangle has hypotenuse thirteen and one leg five. Find the other leg.
steps.okSay: Yes! One sixty-nine minus twenty-five is one forty-four. The square root is twelve.
steps.noSay: Not quite. Thirteen is the hypotenuse, so subtract the squares: one sixty-nine minus twenty-five is one forty-four. The square root is twelve.

steps.html:
Shortcut: famous right triangles

3-4-5×2 → 6-8-105-12-138-15-177-24-25

See two of these numbers in a right triangle? You already know the third. Multiples work too: 6-8-10, 9-12-15.
say: These right triangles show up all the time. Three, four, five. Five, twelve, thirteen. Eight, fifteen, seventeen. And seven, twenty-four, twenty-five.
If you see two of these numbers in a right triangle, you already know the third one. Doubles and triples work too, like six, eight, ten.
Great! Now 4 practice questions. You'll see the answer and an explanation after each one.
Last part: three checkpoint questions. Get two out of three to finish the lesson. You've got this!

steps.html:
Remember

1. Angles in a triangle add to 180°. Subtract the two you know from 180.

2. Isosceles: 2 equal angles. Equilateral: all 60°.

3. Right triangles: a2 + b2 = c2. Missing hypotenuse → add; missing leg → subtract.

4. Know 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.
say: Let's review. The angles of a triangle add to one eighty. Subtract the two you know from one eighty.
Isosceles triangles have two equal angles, and equilateral triangles have three sixty-degree angles.
In a right triangle, a squared plus b squared equals c squared. Missing the hypotenuse, add. Missing a leg, subtract.
And remember the famous triangles: three four five, five twelve thirteen, and eight fifteen seventeen. Great job!
